item.title: How to Prepare to Watch 'The One With Matthew Perry'
item.description:
Relationships

How to Prepare to Watch 'The One With Matthew Perry'

Beyond the sarcasm: Reflecting on the enduring impact of Chandler Bing.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • For many, the allure of fame lies in its promise to alleviate feelings of insignificance.
  • Fame is a poor substitute for love.
  • In his memoir "Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing," the late Matthew Perry spoke candidly about this.

Matthew Perry gave us the beloved character "Chandler Bing." For more than a decade, his sarcasm and quick wit made us laugh, cry, and eventually wonder what happens when the applause ends. Friends is an iconic and nostalgic show that, to many, represents the comforting reality of the "found family"—that beautiful chapter of emerging adulthood when your friends are your primary source of stability, love, and support. The sadness we feel when watching Chandler Bing now stems from a bittersweet mix of his character's tragic upbringing, his defense mechanisms, and the real-world tragedy of the actor who portrayed him, Matthew Perry.

In his memoir Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing, the late Matthew Perry, the actor known for playing the sarcastic but lovable Chandler Bing in the hit TV show Friends, discussed the impacts of his parents’ acrimonious divorce on his emotional well-being as a child. He explains how loyalty binds, conflict, and a sense of being alone created a deep-seated sense of shame and self-blame for him as a child. Perry discussed a childhood of feeling like an outsider looking in on his family, with evasive parents preoccupied with their own personal and professional aspirations. Perry, by his own admission, felt abandoned and unworthy. He never understood why his father chose to leave the family to pursue his dream of becoming an actor in Hollywood and felt that his mother was preoccupied with her “new life” and “new family.” Perry explained that being torn between two parents in two different countries was heartbreaking; he often found himself flying as an unaccompanied minor from the age of 5. On those long, lonely flights, he would try to tell himself that he was embarking on an exciting adventure but on the inside, he felt terrified and forgotten. In his own words, Perry explains:

There was now a family growing up around me, a family I didn’t really feel a part of. It was around this time that I made the conscious choice to say, Fuck it—it’s every man for himself. That’s when the bad behavior started—I got shitty grades, I started smoking, I beat up Pierre’s son (an eventual prime minister himself) Justin Trudeau . . . I made the choice to live in my head and not in my heart. It was safer in my head—you couldn’t be broken there, not yet anyway . . . I was a bad kid.

How Complex Trauma Shapes Self-Image and Relationships

No one is born believing themselves unworthy of love, respect, or comfort; unworthiness is learned through painful life experiences. This death by a thousand cuts is the subtle yet deeply painful experience of complex trauma. Perry identifies as a “bad” or “broken” person many times in his memoir. Research has found that adult survivors of clustered adverse childhood experience go on to develop high-risk maladaptive behaviors, difficulty in establishing and maintaining healthy relationships, mental distress, and poor physical health. Adverse childhood experiences can include growing up in a home in which substance abuse, divorce, mental illness, suicidal ideation, violence, sexual abuse, or criminality are present.

Perry, like so many other children of divorce, explains in his memoir that he felt that he was placed in what is called a “loyalty bind.” Though alliances and conflicts naturally emerge in all family systems within a dysfunctional family system, loyalty binds are especially threatening to a child’s well-being. A child may be forced to take sides in conflicts between parents or between parents and siblings. This can often result in the child feeling forced to choose as a demonstration of loyalty but ultimately feeling deeply shameful. The Adverse Childhood Experiences Study explored the relationship between childhood trauma and long-term health outcomes; in the study, researchers discovered that kids facing multiple challenges in their life are at a higher risk of encountering difficulties such as struggling with emotions, performance in school, relationships, and impulsive behavior as they grow older.

When a person experiences childhood trauma, they may seek comfort in repetitive behaviors that can potentially lead to issues like addiction. Moreover, enduring significant trauma during childhood can contribute to feelings of sadness, increased risk of suicidality, weakened physical health, autoimmune diseases, and the impulse to engage in self-destructive and harmful behaviors. Perry developed several core negative beliefs; in his own words, he viewed himself as “broken, bent, unlovable.” Perry’s childhood marked by loneliness, isolation, and despair reportedly led him to seek solace through substance use in a ritualistic and compulsive manner, which in turn gave rise to a lasting battle with addiction. However, he did feel love on the stage.

The Illusion of Fame as a Substitute for Love

For many, the allure of fame lies in its promise to alleviate feelings of insignificance and fill emotional voids. The adoration and attention that come with fame can temporarily fulfill our emotional need for recognition, validation, and affection. However, fame is a poor substitute for love. While the spotlight of fame can momentarily satisfy the desire for acceptance, true and lasting love and fulfillment are inner journeys that cannot be replaced by external accolades. At 54 years old, Perry died from the acute effects of the anesthetic ketamine. As he wrote in his memoir, “I had a monster in my brain, a monster who wanted to get me alone and convince me to have that first drink or pill, and then that monster would engulf me.” Though I did not have the honor of working with Matthew Perry, his memoir revealed themes emblematic of complex trauma.

As you prepare to return to the nostalgia of Friends and watch Chandler Bing once more, remember that you are witnessing both a brilliant comedic performance and the intricate armor of a man who was fighting a silent, lifelong battle. Matthew Perry’s story is a poignant reminder that the loudest laughs often mask the deepest wounds, and that no amount of external adoration can quiet the challenges born from complex trauma. When you see Chandler use sarcasm to deflect vulnerability, let it serve as a gentle prompt to look closer at your own life and the lives of those around you. Let his legacy inspire you to practice radical compassion—both for the people in your life who might be hiding behind their own wit, and for yourself, if you are still trying to heal the parts of you that felt forgotten as a child. Matthew Perry spent his life trying to make the world feel a little lighter; as you watch him now, honor his memory by choosing to live in your heart rather than your head, and by remembering that you, just as you are, have always been worthy of love.

item.title: AI and People With Brain Injury
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and People With Brain Injury

What are the unique issues AI presents to people with brain injury?

Posted October 22, 2026

Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

Generative AI is AI that creates content, e.g., text, images, video, music, and so on. I, a human being with a brain injury, am writing this post. Psychology Today requires its bloggers to confirm they used no artificial intelligence (AI) before submitting posts for review. I endorse this statement:

“Psychology Today is the international authority on behavioral science in large part because of your unique insight and breadth of knowledge. Using generative AI abdicates this expertise and authority, devalues Psychology Today and impugns your own reputation as a writer and subject matter expert.”

But not all AI is generative, even though generative AI developers have disrupted and dominated the conversation, affecting us all and creating three issues that apply particularly to people with brain injury. According to Galileo AI, which observes and evaluates GenAI apps, agentic AI autonomously pursues goals through “planning, tool use, and execution.” Attie, an alternative to closed AI ecosystems, is an open-source agentic AI that uses Anthropic to generate Attie’s responses that connect to your Atmosphere (ATProto) identity for “exploring and building on the network.” This kind of AI could emancipate people with brain injury wholly or partially from depending on others for daily tasks and online social life. But allowing AI in swirls up questions around privacy and medical confidentiality.

When you have a brain injury with slow processing, poor working memory, and/or concentration deficits, you’ll struggle with understanding why open-source AI empowers you unlike closed ecosystems and how to use AI beneficially while safeguarding your personal information and health data. Organizations that serve people with brain injury may not have thought about AI or don’t understand it and thus cannot guide their clients in safe and effective use. Still, knowing how companies like Meta and Google data mine and how to protect against their intrusions serves as a model for retaining confidentiality when using AI.

Client Privacy

AI requires a large amount of computing power. Neural processing units aid in using AI on laptops, but for the average person, AI computing is done through the cloud, that is, on data servers. EFF’s Surveillance Self-Defense notes the risk: “Depending on the type of tool you’re using, this can mean the company behind that tool can collect a variety of information, ranging from every query you type into a chatbot to the full text of a document or the entirety of a transcribed meeting.” If a privacy statement uses the phrase “reduce the amount of personal information," this does not mean the company eliminates personal information. In the future, someone using the trained model could recover it. So using AI offline on a laptop better safeguards medical information from privacy-breaking initiatives or from the mining and selling of your data.

In that case, the data a person wants an agentic AI to use must also be stored on the laptop: calendar, email, reminders, writing software, documents, images, videos, social media posts, blog posts, etc.

But let’s say you use AI on your phone or old laptop while erroneously assuming the phone’s AI doesn’t depend on the cloud. As Surveillance Self-Defense notes: The only way to determine what is on the cloud is to “try disabling the internet connection on your device then using the AI feature. If it still works, it’s likely an on device feature.” A healthcare provider could then discuss with the client how to adapt their use.

Healthcare Professional-Client Interaction

Some clients are already using AI agents on their phones and laptops and may not consider their health team or caregiver’s privacy when using agentic AI in their homes. They may film them executing a task, ask AI to store and analyze the video, and later ask their AI to replay the video for them to follow. When agentic AI uses cloud computing, the caregiver’s face will be uploaded to the cloud without their permission, along with their name and any other information on them that their client has stored in their contacts or notes. Companies may tie this data to other online data, such as where a healthcare professional shops, their friends and family, which clients they visit, which clinics they work at, and so on. Some people with brain injury may not understand the need for their healthcare team’s or caregiver’s privacy and may swoop in with their phone and ask its AI agent to videotape before the professional can say, “Stop.”

I think we as people with brain injury ought to respect the privacy of healthcare professionals and caregivers and learn to ask for permission each and every time we use AI. This respect also extends to asking permission to name them on social media, upload selfies with them, and so on.

Emancipation

For the tech-minded, open-source AI like Attie provides the possibility of creating apps for our unique needs while understanding what data is collected, how it’s used, and with whom it’s shared. Yet how can the average person keep their medical information private even when their data is not under the control of a closed ecosystem?

We can’t without awareness.

Neither can our service providers.

But organizations such as EFF (Electronic Frontier Foundation) in the US and OpenMedia in Canada can teach us how and keep us current. Brain injury organizations could use EFF’s Surveillance Self-Defense modules to guide their clients on current safe and private use of online activities and agentic AI. OpenMedia calls for plain language to foster understanding.

Healthcare providers need to create and share with clients AI policies within the broader framework of data retention and privacy practices for both staff and clients, but not in a top-down “thou shalt obey or else” tone; no adult appreciates being told off before they’ve done anything wrong or being treated like a child. Instead, approach this issue collaboratively. Collaboration breeds respect and an atmosphere of we’ll mine the best parts of AI together while protecting each other’s privacy.

One final note: People with brain injury do not require AI to write or create art. No matter how long it takes or how arduous the process, we can create beautiful works ourselves.

item.title: Why Resilience Is Not a Solo Act
item.description:
Resilience

Why Resilience Is Not a Solo Act

Understanding the benefits of connection as a solution.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Resilience is more than just learning to bounce back from adversity.
  • It helps to learn coping strategies, but recognizing how the environment creates challenges is also important.
  • There is a difference between getting through challenges and allowing yourself to stay in unsafe situations.
  • Leaning on support, connection, and community is vital for enhancing resilience.

What do you think of when you hear the word resilience?

The number one answer is “bouncing back!” We often think of the person who keeps on going even when times are hard, or the person who gets knocked down and gets back up. They are the ones who adapt, find their way forward, and always keep it moving.

These days, resilience has become central in most conversations about mental health and well-being. We are all struggling with uncertainty, stress, change, and an overwhelming constant stream of information about what’s happening in the world. Science says that coping with difficult circumstances is an important part of taking care of ourselves.

The trouble is, sometimes we define resilience too narrowly. We focus more on whether someone can keep going and forget to ask, “How are you really doing?”

Research about resilience has raised an important question: Is adapting to difficult circumstances the same as being well?

Coping Is the Goal

Given all this is happening in the world, we have become pretty good at functioning under stress. We are able to go to work, take care of our families, meet most of our responsibilities, and continue to show up for those around us. The trouble is, just because we’re still functioning, we assume that we’re doing fine.

The issue is that functioning is not the same as doing well. To better understand why simply functioning is not enough, consider the concept of weathering, which describes how prolonged and ongoing exposure to stress often accumulates over time and negatively impacts our bodies. Weathering research demonstrates the difference between repeatedly responding to difficult circumstances and flourishing in life.

It explains why someone can be productive and dependable while also being exhausted and overwhelmed. We are generally able to adapt to unhealthy situations even when those situations are not healthy for us.

As a certified resiliency advocate, I am always cautious when resilience is presented as something people need to develop within themselves. While there are many skills that we can learn to help us manage stress, it’s important to recognize that our relationships, workplaces, families, and communities significantly influence our mental health and well-being.

My point is that the question cannot only be “How can I handle this difficult situation better?” It must also be “What is happening around me that is making life so difficult, and what support will help me get through it?”

It’s OK When Life Is Hard

Let’s be clear. I’m not saying resilience means we should create a life of ease. Without discomfort, we would not grow. It’s an important aspect of life to have that difficult conversation, try something new, or make that challenging decision.

Having said that, recent work on resilience suggests that we “microdose” discomfort into our lives regularly. So, rather than avoiding challenges altogether, we should practice experiencing small amounts of discomfort designed to help us build confidence to get through challenges. The goal is to put ourselves in minimally stressful situations, such as putting our phone away, speaking up in crowds, or trying something new.

The distinction is that there is a difference between a little healthy discomfort and ongoing chronic stressful situations. For example, learning to have a difficult conversation is very different from learning to tolerate a toxic relationship. Becoming comfortable with change is not the same as staying in a harmful situation. One builds your muscle while the other tears you down.

In the End, We Still Need Each Other

So, how can we get through challenging times? One important protective factor is having access to social connections. Connections help us get through challenging times and provide the support that we need.

Connection is not simply access to people. Real connection requires relationships where we feel seen, known, supported, and like we belong. Examples include a community gathering, sharing a meal with someone, or just meeting a friend for coffee.

When we talk about resilience as though it is built inside of a person, we are forgetting about how protective factors support us during difficult times. For many of us, our relationships are part of how we get through the tough stuff. When we are feeling overwhelmed, having someone to call changes our experience. When we need to feel grounded, a community gives us a sense of stability. Just knowing that people will notice our struggles makes it easier to ask for help.

While resilience is very personal, we rarely practice it alone.

Can We Touch Resilience?

Resilience means a lot of different things to different people. For some it means getting through; for others it means asking for help. The key is to know what your skills are and when you need to focus on building new ones.

We don’t want to focus on “How resilient am I?” but rather, “What is helping me stay healthy?” or “Who can I turn to?”

In the end, resilience is not about how much we can handle. It’s really about what we’re doing to take care of ourselves, how we connect with others, and whether we are in situations that allow us to thrive.

item.title: Why You Are Drawn to Partners Who Need 'Fixing'
item.description:
Narcissism

Why You Are Drawn to Partners Who Need 'Fixing'

How narcissistic parents nourish the savior complex.

Posted October 22, 2026

As I’ve sat across from many people who are empathetic, giving, and caring, I’ve heard them ask the same question over and over again: "Why, why do I keep falling for people I have to save?!”

Their dating history looks less like courtship and more like scavenging: the addicted, the financially unstable, or the emotionally unavailable. And they always carry the same belief: With enough love and patience, my loved one will finally become the partner I deserve.

You can call it the Savior Trap.

It has nothing to do with bad luck, nor with poor judgment. This pattern began long before the first date. To understand why you seek out the broken, we need to look at what happened when you were small.

The Child as a Commodity

In a healthy family, a child is a subject—a person with valid feelings, desires, and boundaries. In a narcissistic family, the child is something else, namely an extension, a function, or a commodity meant to meet the parent's needs.

Dan Shaw describes this traumatic narcissism as a relational system in which the parent seeks control over the child's inner life to regulate their own fragile self-esteem.

As a child, you were drafted into roles you were never meant to hold. You were cast as the friend-therapist, listening to your mother's marital problems. You were the emotional regulator, walking on eggshells to prevent your father's rage. So, you learned early that your value was tied to your usefulness, and that to be loved means to be useful.

Over time, this became a belief: I exist to help. I am loved for what I do, not for who I am. And the better I save someone, or endeavor to fix their life, the more they value my presence.

Why "Broken" Feels Familiar

If you grew up believing your job was to fix your parent's inner world, then a healthy, stable partner can feel very strange. Almost boring. You seek out the broken because they feel familiar. They just feel like home.

There are four reasons for this.

  1. The Illusion of Control. When you take on the role of Savior, you find someone with struggles and devote yourself to their improvement. This creates a power balance that feels safe to you. As long as they need you, they will not leave. As long as they are broken, you remain indispensable.
  2. The Avoidance of Yourself. By focusing on your partner's crisis, you can avoid looking at your own wounds or past traumas. Fixing someone else is a distraction from the shame and emptiness that might linger from your childhood.
  3. The Hope for Redemption. Part of you is trying to win a battle you lost years ago. By saving a broken or dysfunctional partner, you are trying to prove you are finally good enough to earn the love your parent withheld. The true addressee of the fullness of your care isn't your partner but instead your parent, whose love you continue to crave.
  4. The Familiar Rhythm of Chaos. A home shaped by narcissism is unpredictable. You never knew which version of your parent would greet you: will it be the charming one or the cruel one today? That unpredictability wired your nervous system to equate intensity with intimacy. A partner who brings calm feels flat, but one who brings drama feels like love. So, you are drawn to chaos because it has become the only rhythm your body knows.

The Price of the Rescue

The Savior Trap is self-sabotaging because without a crisis to manage, you no longer know how to relate. Even when the fixer-upper starts to get better—e.g., they find a job or overcome an addiction—Savior, who devoted everything to this moment, may feel empty, or even irritated. Automatically, you stay stuck in what Shaw calls a "relational system of subjugation," in which your partner’s autonomy feels like betrayal because your autonomy was deemed betrayal by your parents.

Healing the Wound in Four Steps

Better dating strategies don’t really cure the Savior Trap. Consider the following steps instead.

Step 1: Legalizing the Anger. Many adult children of narcissists feel guilty for being angry at their parents. But anger is a normal response to having your boundaries violated. You need to grieve the parent you never had and the childhood you sacrificed. And grieving includes expressing and dealing with your anger about the dear thing you've either lost or never had.

Step 2: Rewrite the Introjected Voice. You need to identify the parental voice inside your head that tells you that you are selfish for having needs. This means entering a dialogue with this voice and setting boundaries, both within yourself and with others. It will include learning that no is pretty much a complete sentence.

Step 3: Learning to Tolerate Calm. If chaos has been your baseline, peace will feel wrong at first. You may interpret a partner's steadiness as indifference, or you may find yourself provoking conflict just to feel something familiar. This phase is for retraining your nervous system to accept safety without sabotaging it.

Step 4: The Non-Narcissistic Relationship. Therapy often becomes your first experience of a relationship where you are not being used. In this space, the therapist provides what we call affective mirroring—seeing you for who you are, not for what you can do.

If you find yourself in the Savior Trap, remember that your desire to help is a good part of you. You don’t need to divest yourself of it and become selfish or egotistical. But it was forged in a fire you were never meant to endure, one that engendered the habit of fixing and saving others, at the expense of your own well-being. And this habit is worth “fixing.”
